title: A Resilient Water System
premise: Help a remote community design a reliable, low-maintenance water system before the next dry season.
impact: A practical solution here could provide clean water, stronger food production, and greater independence for the community.

chapters.title: Is the spring enough?
chapters.scene: The village sits below a spring that has never run dry. In the dry season its flow drops to its lowest, and the council's first question is simple: will it be enough? A villager times how long the spring takes to fill a 20-liter bucket.
givens: A 20-liter bucket fills in 250 seconds at the spring in the dry season.
chapters.question: How many liters does the spring give in a full day of the dry season?
chapters.method: 20 liters in 250 seconds is 0.08 liters a second. 0.08 × 60 × 60 × 24 = 6,912 liters a day.

right.text: 6,912 liters a day. Two hundred people at 20 liters each need about 4,000 liters a day, so the spring is enough, with room to spare.

wrong.text: The council sends someone back up to time the bucket again before anyone will commit. Five days lost.

data: About 200 people live in the village.
Basic access to water is usually reckoned at about 20 liters per person per day.

chapters.title: The drop
chapters.scene: The spring is 45 meters higher than the place in the village where the taps will go. With no pumps, that height is what moves the water. Before choosing a pipe, you need to know how hard the water will push on it at the bottom when every tap is closed.
givens: Height of the spring above the taps: 45 meters
chapters.question: What static pressure, in kilopascals, will the water have at the taps when nothing is flowing?
chapters.method: Pressure = density × gravity × height = 1,000 × 9.81 × 45 = 441,450 pascals, about 441 kPa, or 4.4 bar. Every 10 meters of height adds about 1 bar.

right.text: About 441 kPa, or 4.4 bar. Whatever pipe runs along the lowest stretch has to hold at least that, with a margin.

wrong.text: Your number goes into the report as it is. It will matter when you choose the pipe.

data: The pipe runs 1.2 km from the spring, mostly downhill, with its lowest point at the village.

chapters.title: Choosing the pipe
chapters.scene: Three suppliers have quoted for 1.2 km of pipe. Whatever you choose has to be carried up the mountain path, laid in a trench, and hold the pressure at the bottom for years with almost no maintenance.

options.label: Plastic pipe (HDPE), rated PN4
options.detail: Light coils, quick to lay. Rated for 4 bar. $9,000, about 35 days to install.
options.outcome: The coils go up the path quickly. The rating is printed on every meter: 4 bar.

options.label: Plastic pipe (HDPE), rated PN6
options.detail: Light coils, quick to lay. Rated for 6 bar. $12,000, about 35 days to install.
options.outcome: The coils go up the path quickly: 6 bar on every meter, a comfortable margin over the 4.4 bar at the bottom.

options.label: Galvanized steel pipe
options.detail: Very strong, but heavy, in 6-meter lengths that must be joined, and it can rust where the coating is damaged. $26,000, about 60 days to install.
options.outcome: It will hold any pressure here, but every length has to be carried up and threaded by hand.

chapters.explain: Tell the council why you chose it.
rubric: compares each pipe's rating with the pressure at the bottom (about 4.4 bar)
leaves a safety margin above that pressure
weighs the cost against a budget that must also pay for storage and taps
considers carrying, installing and maintaining it in a remote place
data: PN ratings give the pressure, in bar, a pipe is designed to hold continuously.
HDPE pipe is light and flexible, comes in long coils, and lasts for decades buried.
Galvanized steel comes in 6-meter lengths joined by threaded couplings.
The budget also has to pay for a storage tank, tap stands, fittings and labor.

chapters.title: An unexpected expense

event.text: The cement supplier writes: prices are up 25%. The storage tank you planned for $8,000 will now cost $10,000.

chapters.scene: Share out what's left of the budget. The village wants water at four tap stands, a tank that holds three days of water for when the pipe needs repair, and something left over to fix things later.

buckets.label: Storage tank (three days of water)
buckets.short: A smaller tank: if the pipe breaks, the village has less than three days of water.

buckets.label: Four tap stands ($1,500 each)
buckets.short: Fewer tap stands: longer walks and longer queues.

buckets.label: Fittings and labor
buckets.short: Too few hands: the work goes slower, about 15 days more.

buckets.label: Repair reserve
buckets.short: Nothing set aside for the first repair.

chapters.explain: What did you protect, and what did you give up?
rubric: fits the total within the budget left
keeps three days of storage in case the pipe fails
explains what was cut, if anything, and why that cut does the least harm
data: Three days of water for 200 people at 20 liters each is 12,000 liters.
Ferrocement tanks are built on site from cement, sand and wire mesh.
Each tap stand serves about 50 people.

chapters.title: The approaching storm

event.text: A storm is forecast in three days. The trench across the steep slope above the village is half dug, and the village is running low on supplies.

chapters.scene: Rain on an open trench can wash the slope, and the pipe in it, away. But every day you wait is a day closer to the dry season, and families are already rationing water.

options.label: Keep working through the storm
options.detail: No time lost now, but an open trench on a steep slope in heavy rain.
options.outcome: The rain comes harder than forecast. Part of the slope slides into the trench, and a section of pipe has to be dug out and relaid: twelve days.

options.label: Stop and secure the site
options.detail: Cover the trench, anchor the pipe, bring the crew down. About 7 days lost.
options.outcome: The storm passes over a covered trench. A week lost, nothing broken.

options.label: Reroute along the ridge
options.detail: A longer, safer line: 300 meters more pipe ($3,000) and about 10 days.
options.outcome: The longer line costs more, but it no longer crosses the slope that slides.

chapters.explain: Tell the crew what you've decided, and why.
rubric: weighs the risk to the pipe against the days lost
considers how much time is left before the dry season
considers the village's needs while waiting
data: Landslides are most likely on steep slopes with loose, wet soil.
The crew is ten volunteers from the village.

endings.title: A burst at the bottom
endings.text: Water reaches the village on the first day. Then, at the lowest stretch, the pipe splits: at 4.4 bar, the water there pushes harder than PN4 pipe is made to hold. The council finds the money to replace the bottom section, but the village carries water through the first weeks of the dry season. It's the lesson every water engineer learns early: rate the pipe for its lowest point, with a margin.

endings.title: Not before the dry season
endings.text: The work runs past the first dry weeks. The system is finished, and it works, but the village carried water for a while yet.

endings.title: Water, with strain
endings.text: Water runs at the taps before the dry season. Something you couldn't afford, or a setback you couldn't avoid, will be felt: longer queues, less water stored, or no money for the first repair. A working system, with less margin than the village hoped for.

endings.title: Water before the dry season
endings.text: Water runs at all four tap stands weeks before the dry season, from a pipe rated well above the pressure it carries, a tank that holds three days, and money set aside for repairs. Two hundred people stop carrying water up the hill.
